I found nothing at all on vv. 20–21, nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org or the Catholic and Orthodox sites, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings. Every point below comes from pages I actually read. Older commentators like Gill and Calvin are cited at the page where I read them.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Returning to God meant getting rid of the idols. Guzik compares this to an unfaithful spouse who can't keep a lover and still truly come home. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Clarke reads "you shall not be moved" (BSB: "no longer waver") as a promise that if they repented they would not be taken into captivity. So even a judgment God had announced could have been avoided. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-4.html
- Matthew Henry says sin has to be removed from the heart, because only then is it out of God's sight. He also notes that some read the phrase as "you must not wander back" to idols. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm

**v. 2:** Henry: swearing "in truth, justice and righteousness" means never using an oath to back up something false, uncertain or unintended. He also says Israel's return would draw the nations to put their happiness in God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm
- Clarke: the nations would be so struck by God's change in Israel that their usual blessing would become "May the God of Israel bless you." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-2.html
- Barnes draws two lessons: Gentiles were to belong to the Messiah's church, and Israel was meant to be God's go-between in that work. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) says the nations' conversion follows Israel's (citing Rom 11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-2.htm

**v. 3:** The "fallow ground" is a hardened heart that needs real, costly repentance, not a show. Guzik adds that unplowed fields don't grow nothing; they grow weeds and thorns. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Clarke: let repentance break up the hard heart, and once the word is sown, don't let worldly cares choke it like thorns. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-4.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: the thorns are the evil desires of an unrenewed heart, as in Matthew 13:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-4.htm

**v. 4:** The picture changes from farming to circumcision, the sign of Abraham's covenant. What must be cut away is the "foreskin of the heart." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Pulpit: every Jew was circumcised, but not all were "circumcised to the Lord." Jeremiah is fighting a purely ritual view of the rite, under the influence of Deuteronomy 10:16, and Paul says the same in Romans 2:28–29. Ellicott: the "foreskin of the heart" is the unrenewed, fleshly nature. The Cambridge Bible says this inward circumcision points ahead to Jeremiah's New Covenant (31:31–34). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-4.htm
- Calvin: circumcision always stood for self-denial, so the people had no excuse of ignorance. Their circumcision had become something to boast about in front of others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-4.html
- Henry: God's wrath is what we should fear most, and it is our own evil deeds that light it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm

**vv. 5–6:** Henry: "God's usual method is to warn before he wounds." The alarm was spread widely so the people would either repent or be left without excuse. Those able to fight were to hold the fortified cities, and the weak were to leave. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm
- Guzik, quoting Cundall: Jeremiah writes as if the judgment were already happening, because it is so certain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/

**v. 7:** The "lion" was fulfilled in the Babylonian conquest. Guzik notes the debate over Scythians, Assyrians or Babylonians, and sides with Babylon, following Kidner. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Henry names the lion as Nebuchadnezzar: the destroyer of the Gentiles becomes the destroyer of the Jews once they have made themselves like the Gentiles. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm

**v. 8:** Guzik: this pictures the people finally repenting, but too late to stop the judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/

**v. 9:** The leaders lose heart, and the priests and prophets are at a loss because they never answered God's call to return. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Henry: sin takes away a person's confidence before God, and with it their courage before others. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm

**v. 10:** Most say the promise "You will have peace" came from the false prophets, not from God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/ and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-10.html (Coffman)
- Henry: God deceives no one. The people fooled themselves, and the false prophets fooled them. Henry adds that the verse can also be read as a question. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm
- Readings differ here; see Part 2.

**vv. 11–12:** The desert wind is not a gentle one for winnowing or cleansing. It is too strong for that, and it destroys. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Bridgeway: God's judgment burns his people up like a scorching desert wind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-10.html

**v. 13:** The invaders' speed shows they cannot be stopped. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/

**v. 14:** Judah's repentance had been only for show (3:10), so Jeremiah calls for washing the heart, not just outward actions. Thompson observes that Jeremiah never treated a call to repent as too late. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Henry: no reform saves unless it reaches the heart. He compares outward fixes to treating leprosy with ointment alone, and says "how long" shows God thinks the delay is long. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm

**vv. 15–17:** Henry says the "watchers" (BSB: "besieging army") from a far country are soldiers waiting for any chance to do harm. The warning is told to the nations but aimed at Jerusalem. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm
- Guzik: the coming army is why the plea to repent is so urgent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/

**v. 18:** The judgment would be their own fault, not a failure on God's part. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Henry: sin is the cause of all our troubles, and the problem was a whole way of life, not one or two slips. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm

**v. 19:** Henry: the prophet cries out like someone in great pain or a woman in labour, though he himself is well. He grieves for the nation, not for himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm
- Ellicott: the Hebrews saw the "bowels" (BSB: "anguish") as the seat of strong feeling, and the verb is often used for labour pains. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-19.htm
- Clarke says vv. 19–29 describe the ruin with imagery "scarcely paralleled in the whole Bible." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-19.html
- Who is speaking is debated; see Part 2.

**v. 22:** God says plainly that they are foolish and do not know him, yet he still calls them "My people." They are clever only at evil. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Henry: those who are called God's people and still don't know him are the most foolish of all. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm

**v. 23:** "Formless and void" (*tohu vabohu*) uses the words of Genesis 1:2. Creation is run backwards. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Calvin: through their sins the Jews had overturned the order of nature. Clarke and Constable say the same about the Genesis wording. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-23.html
- Barnes: the imagery is that of the last day of judgment. Gill: "the earth" here means the land of Judea, not the whole world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-23.htm
- The verse also comes up in a creation debate; see Part 3.

**vv. 24–26:** Henry: the darkened heavens recall Genesis 1:2 and the darkness at Christ's death. Ruined cities "before the LORD" show the true cause behind the invaders. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm
- JFB: repeating "I looked" four times deepens the effect. Blaney, quoted by Benson, describes even the birds leaving the fields. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-23.htm
- Clarke on v. 25: the birds left because there was no food. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-4.html

**v. 27:** Judgment would not be complete. Kidner says this saving clause "shines very brightly." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Henry: God would keep a remnant, and Jerusalem would be rebuilt. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm
- Coffman contrasts this with Nineveh, of which God did make a "full end." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-27.html

**v. 28:** Keil & Delitzsch: the desolation rests on a decree God will not take back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-27.htm
- Pulpit: the decree is fixed, but there is "a gleam of hope." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-30.html

**v. 29:** Henry: every city is abandoned, and government and trade come to an end. Don't love your houses too much, because rocks and thickets may one day be the safer place. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_004.cfm

**v. 30:** Zion is pictured as a woman dressed up to win over her invaders. Outward show and false confidence cannot replace repentance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-4/
- Matthew Henry (Concise): no outward privilege or scheme would prevent the destruction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/4.htm

**v. 31:** Clarke: the first birth was thought the most painful and dangerous, and spreading the hands is the natural sign of distress and a plea for help. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-4.html
- The "Daughter of Zion" is a female picture of weakness, also used in Isaiah 1:8 and Lamentations 1:6. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/4.htm

---

## 2. Where Protestant interpreters really differ

I found no clear lines between denominations in this chapter. The real disagreements are between individual commentators. Where the source labels them, I've given their tradition.

**v. 10: in what sense did God "deceive"?** Three readings:
- **God's judicial hardening.** God allowed, and even sent, the false prophets as a judgment, as with Ahab's lying prophets in 1 Kings 22. This is the view of Keil & Delitzsch, the Geneva Bible notes (Reformed), and Benson (Methodist), who also cites 2 Thessalonians 2:11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-10.htm
- **Irony.** Calvin (Reformed) says Jeremiah is mocking the false prophets and the people, not blaming God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-10.html
- **A real, puzzled complaint.** Clarke (Wesleyan) thinks Jeremiah could not square the ruin with earlier promises. Constable says Jeremiah objected because God had allowed false prophets to promise peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-10.html
- Ellicott takes a similar line. The prophets had spoken in God's name, so had God not seemingly deceived the people? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-10.htm

**v. 19: who is speaking?**
- Most say the prophet himself: Henry, Clarke (Wesleyan), Poole, and the Geneva notes, which say true ministers feel the church's suffering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-19.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-19.html
- Barnes (labelled Presbyterian) hears the people grieving. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-19.html
- JFB says the prophet speaks as the nation personified. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-19.htm
- Calvin says it is not mainly Jeremiah's own grief. It is a description written to wake up careless hearers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-19.html

**v. 2: is this about Christ?**
- Gill (Baptist): the nations are blessed in the Messiah, the Lord Jesus. He rejects the rabbis' view that it means "in Israel." Benson calls it a prediction of gospel times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-2.htm
- Clarke reads it more simply, as the nations' form of blessing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-2.html
- Calvin also rejects applying the phrase to Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-2.html

**v. 4: a Reformed covenant emphasis.** Ligonier says the people could not trust the outward sign for covenant blessing. They needed the inner reality it stands for, because God's covenant "has always been a covenant of the heart." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/circumcision-heart

**v. 27: hope, or more punishment?**
- Most read "I will not make a full end" as the promise of a remnant.
- Poole mentions a reading that means "I'm not finished with you yet," that is, more punishment is coming. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-27.htm
- Calvin says he prefers a reading like that (no let-up in vengeance), though his editor's note defends the remnant meaning. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-27.html

---

## 3. Other views (only what I found)

**v. 27, critical scholarship.** The Cambridge Bible thinks "yet I will not make a full end" was probably added later, because it breaks the metre and the flow of vv. 27–28. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/4-27.htm

**v. 23, the "gap theory."** This is a popular creation teaching, made famous by the Scofield Reference Bible. It uses Jeremiah 4:23 to argue that the earth "became" formless after a catastrophe between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2. https://biblehub.com/q/what's_the_biblical_gap_theory.htm
- John MacArthur (GTY) rejects it. He says Jeremiah uses Genesis wording to describe Judah ruined by judgment, and that the theory contradicts Exodus 20:11. https://www.gty.org/blogs/print/B170503/the-gaping-holes-in-the-gap-theory
- Don Stewart argues that Jeremiah's judgment setting shouldn't be read back into Genesis, where there is no judgment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/faq/don_stewart/don_stewart_654.cfm

**Jewish reading (v. 10).** The Targum, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase quoted by Clarke and Gill, puts the deceiving on the false prophets and not on God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/4-10.html

**Not found:** netbible.org notes, bibleodyssey.org, Catholic or Orthodox readings, and any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. BibleHub lists Haydock (a Catholic commentary) on its verse pages, but I couldn't get to its text, so I've left it out.
